Class 6 · Module 2 — Organ Systems on the Panel

The Liver's Alarm Bells — and False Alarms

ALT and AST are honest sentinels that lie about their source. Learn to read the pattern, and to blame the barbell before the liver.

60 min read 8 cited sources

A physically active 39-year-old man walks into his primary care office. He feels fine. But his routine bloodwork shows liver enzymes running 1.4 to 2.3 times above the reference range. What follows is a cascade: hepatitis serologies, an abdominal ultrasound, a referral to gastroenterology. Thousands of dollars and weeks of quiet dread later, someone finally asks him to stop exercising for a week and repeat the test. The numbers glide back to normal. The culprit was never his liver. It was his last hard workout (Tiller & Stringer, 2023).

This is not a rare story. It is one of the most common — and most avoidable — false alarms in all of laboratory medicine. And it happens because two of the liver's most famous markers share a dirty secret: one of them isn't really about the liver at all.

The one-minute version

Before we build the reasoning, here is the payload — the actionable core you can carry into any conversation about liver enzymes.

ALT and AST are enzymes that live inside cells and leak into the blood when those cells are stressed or damaged. They are not measures of what the liver is doing; they are leak detectors. That distinction runs through this entire chapter.

ALT is fairly liver-specific. AST is not — it also pours out of skeletal muscle. So a hard resistance session, a long run, or a bout of unaccustomed training in the 48 to 72 hours before your draw can push AST up and mimic a liver problem that isn't there (Pettersson et al., 2007).

The single most useful discipline in this chapter is timing. What you did in the two to three days before the needle went in is part of the result, whether or not anyone wrote it on the requisition. And the second most useful discipline is to read the two enzymes together — as a relationship — rather than staring at either number alone.

Think About It

If a friend texts you a photo of their lab report with "my AST is high, should I be worried?" — what is the very first question you should ask before saying anything about the liver?

What ALT and AST actually are

Both enzymes are aminotransferases (older reports call them transaminases). Their day job inside a cell is to shuttle nitrogen-containing amino groups between molecules — a routine, essential part of how cells handle amino acids and feed the machinery of energy metabolism. You do not need the biochemistry to use them. You need one idea: they belong inside cells, and finding a lot of them outside — floating in serum — means cells somewhere have become leaky.

Their full names tell you where they live:

ALT — alanine aminotransferase

ALT is concentrated overwhelmingly in the liver. There are trace amounts elsewhere, but for practical purposes, when serum ALT rises, you are looking at a signal from hepatocytes — liver cells. This relative specificity is exactly what makes ALT the more trustworthy of the two when the question is "is this the liver?"

AST — aspartate aminotransferase

AST is generous with its address. It is abundant in the liver, yes — but also in skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle, red blood cells, the kidneys, and the brain. That distribution is the whole reason this chapter exists. AST cannot tell you, by itself, which tissue it came from. A high AST is a question, not an answer.

A crucial historical footnote frames everything that follows. The very phrase "liver function test," or LFT, is what one classic author called a physiological misnomer (invoked in Tiller & Stringer, 2023). ALT and AST do not measure liver function. A perfectly functioning liver can have elevated enzymes, and a badly failing liver can, late in its decline, have deceptively normal ones. These are damage-and-leak markers wearing a misleading label.

"In range" versus "what's normal for you"

Reference ranges for ALT and AST are wider and murkier than most people assume. For years, many labs set the upper limit of normal for ALT around 40 IU/L or higher — a number derived, in part, from populations that included people with undiagnosed fatty liver and other quiet conditions. In other words, the "normal" was partly built from the not-quite-healthy.

When researchers isolated genuinely healthy people, the true healthy-normal ceilings came in strikingly lower: roughly 29 to 33 IU/L for men and 19 to 25 IU/L for women (Kwo et al., 2017). That is a meaningful gap. A man with an ALT of 38 might be told he is "in range" by his lab's cutoff while sitting well above the healthy-population ceiling.

This is the course's recurring lesson in a new costume: "in range" is a statistical statement about a lab's reference population, not a personal verdict of optimal. It does not mean you are fine, and a value just over the line does not mean you are sick. It means the number deserves context — your sex, your training, your medications, your recent history — before it means anything at all.

Think About It

Why might a reference range built from a general population systematically set the "normal" ceiling for ALT too high? What kind of people quietly inflate the upper end?

The relationship is the message

Here is the shift that separates casual readers from skilled ones. Do not read ALT and AST as two independent scores. Read the relationship between them — specifically, how AST compares to ALT. Clinicians formalize this as the AST/ALT ratio, also called the De Ritis ratio after Fernando De Ritis, who described it in 1957 (Botros & Sikaris, 2013).

Why should a simple ratio carry information the two numbers don't carry alone? The answer is elegant and lives in the enzymes' half-lives. AST clears from the blood in roughly 18 hours; ALT lingers about twice as long, around 36 hours (Botros & Sikaris, 2013). Because the two are washed out at different speeds, the shape of their relationship encodes something about the time course and character of whatever caused the leak — not just its size.

Broadly, the general patterns clinicians recognize look like this. Treat them as orientation, never as a diagnosis you assign yourself:

Ratio below 1 (ALT higher than AST)

When ALT sits above AST, the pattern points, in general terms, toward the kinds of liver stress that are common in the modern population — including the fat-related liver changes tied to metabolic risk. This is often the picture in early, chronic, low-grade elevations. It still warrants evaluation, but it is a different flavor of signal than the one below.

Ratio around or above 2 (AST much higher than ALT)

A high ratio — AST running two or more times ALT — is classically associated with more advanced liver injury patterns. A key study of drinkers found that most heavy drinkers without severe liver disease had a ratio at or below 1, whereas 69% of those with cirrhosis had a ratio of 2 or more (Nyblom et al., 2004). The lesson the authors drew is subtle and important: a high ratio flags advanced disease, not merely heavy exposure. The ratio is telling you about the stage and aggressiveness of a process, not simply that it exists.

But — and this is where the field earns its nuance — the simple folk rules ("AST > ALT means alcohol; ALT > AST means viral") are, in the words of the definitive review, too simplistic (Botros & Sikaris, 2013). The ratio is a pattern to be interpreted in context, alongside the absolute values and the whole person. Its usefulness now reaches well beyond the liver into cardiac and muscular conditions too (comprehensive review, 2024). Which brings us to the great confounder.

The confounder that trips up almost everyone: muscle

You met this idea in the metabolic chapter, where recent exercise complicated the picture. Here it returns with even more force, because now it is not just nudging a number — it can produce results that look genuinely alarming.

The landmark demonstration is worth knowing in detail. Fifteen healthy men performed a single weightlifting session. Afterward, their AST, ALT, lactate dehydrogenase, creatine kinase, and myoglobin all rose — and stayed elevated for at least seven days (Pettersson et al., 2007). Some of the "liver function tests" reached values the authors described as highly pathological. In perfectly healthy men. From lifting weights.

But the same study handed us the tool to see through the illusion. While AST and ALT climbed, three other liver-associated markers — bilirubin, GGT, and ALP — stayed comfortably within normal range (Pettersson et al., 2007). That divergence is a fingerprint. Genuine liver disease tends to disturb this broader group; muscle-driven leakage generally does not touch them. When AST rises but the cholestatic markers stay quiet, a muscle source moves up the list of explanations.

Note the asymmetry you should expect. Because ALT is more liver-specific, it moves less from exercise than AST does. So the exercise signature is often a disproportionate AST bump — pushing the AST/ALT ratio upward for reasons that have nothing to do with the liver. This is precisely why reading the ratio without asking about training can send you down the wrong path.

Think About It

In the Pettersson study, why is the fact that bilirubin, GGT, and ALP stayed normal more informative than the fact that AST went up? What does the combination let you rule in or out that AST alone cannot?

Timing: the two days that hide inside every result

If muscle-derived AST can stay elevated for a week, then when you trained relative to the draw is not trivia — it is part of the measurement. A blood test is a snapshot, and the snapshot includes the aftershocks of whatever you did before it.

Practical timing wisdom follows directly:

  • The 48–72 hour window matters most. An intense, unaccustomed, or eccentric-heavy session in the two to three days before a draw is the highest-yield thing to ask about — for yourself or when helping someone make sense of a result.
  • Novelty and intensity beat routine. A workout that is much harder than usual, or a movement pattern the body isn't adapted to, produces bigger leaks than the same person's habitual training.
  • Guideline bodies already acknowledge this. The foundational AGA review notes that ALT can vary day-to-day with exercise and that AST may be affected by exercise (Green & Flamm, 2002). This is not fringe knowledge; it is written into the reference literature.

The actionable move is almost embarrassingly simple. If a liver panel matters to you and you want a clean read, avoid hard or unusual training for two to three days beforehand. And if an elevated AST turns up unexpectedly, recent training is one of the first benign explanations to consider — not the last, after an ultrasound and a specialist referral (Tiller & Stringer, 2023). The knowledge gap the case-report authors lament is exactly this: a workup that never once asked, "have you been training hard lately?"

Worked examples: reading in context

Patterns come alive in cases. Each of these is an interpretation exercise, not a diagnosis. The goal is to reason well enough to know what to do next — which is almost never "panic" and almost never "ignore it."

Case 1 — The alarming AST after leg day

A 34-year-old recreational lifter gets routine labs. AST is 95 (elevated), ALT is 52 (mildly elevated), giving a ratio near 1.8. She feels great. On questioning, she did a heavy squat and deadlift session two days before the draw — her first back after a month off.

Reading: The disproportionate AST, the high-ish ratio, the recent unaccustomed heavy lifting, and the absence of symptoms all point toward a muscle-driven leak. The sensible next step is not an ultrasound; it is to repeat the panel after seven days without hard training, ideally with CK checked alongside (Pettersson et al., 2007; Tiller & Stringer, 2023). If the numbers normalize, the story is complete. If they don't, the question stays open and belongs with a clinician.

Case 2 — The quiet ALT that outruns AST

A 51-year-old man who does not train hard has an ALT of 61 and an AST of 40 — ratio about 0.65 — on two separate draws months apart. He carries extra weight around the middle and has borderline glucose numbers from an earlier chapter.

Reading: Persistent, exercise-independent, ALT-predominant elevation in someone with metabolic risk is a pattern that genuinely warrants medical evaluation (Giboney, 2005; Kwo et al., 2017). There is no muscle story to explain it away. This is not a number to interpret and file — it is a number to bring to a professional, who will take a full history including alcohol, medications, and metabolic factors.

Case 3 — The number just over the line

A 29-year-old woman has an ALT of 24 — under her lab's cutoff of 33, but at the very top of the true healthy-female range. No symptoms, no risk factors, no recent unusual exercise.

Reading: This is the "in range but worth noting" zone. Nothing here demands action, but it is a reasonable value to keep an eye on over time rather than dismiss because it cleared the lab's generous cutoff (Kwo et al., 2017). Trend beats snapshot.

Think About It

Cases 1 and 2 both have elevated enzymes. What single feature most cleanly separates the benign story from the one that needs a doctor — and why is asking about it free?

When to stop interpreting and get help

Interpreting is not diagnosing. Your job as an informed reader is to know which patterns you can reasonably attribute to context and which patterns should hand off to a professional. Escalate — meaning seek medical evaluation rather than self-explanation — when you see:

  • Markedly high values (many times the upper limit), which the guidelines grade as moderate-to-severe and which have their own urgent workup pathways (Kwo et al., 2017).
  • Any symptoms — jaundice, dark urine, right-upper-quadrant pain, unusual fatigue, nausea. Symptoms change everything.
  • Persistent elevation that does not resolve after removing the obvious confounder (i.e., it's still up after a genuine week off hard training).
  • An ALT-predominant pattern with metabolic risk, which has no muscle alibi (Giboney, 2005).
  • Disturbance in the broader panel — abnormal bilirubin, GGT, or ALP alongside the aminotransferases — which points away from a simple muscle leak (Pettersson et al., 2007).

And escalate more calmly — a repeat draw after a training break, with muscle markers checked — when the picture is an isolated AST bump, no symptoms, normal cholestatic markers, and a recent hard or unusual workout. The guidelines themselves endorse this stepwise, history-first approach precisely so people are spared the anxiety and cost of Case-study-in-the-hook workups (Kwo et al., 2017; Green & Flamm, 2002).

Intensive muscular exercise should be considered a cause of asymptomatic elevations in "liver function tests" in clinical practice.

Pettersson et al. (2007)

Key Takeaways

  • ALT and AST are leakage enzymes — they signal that cells are stressed or damaged, not what the liver is functionally doing. "Liver function test" is a misnomer.
  • ALT is fairly liver-specific; AST is not — it also comes from skeletal muscle, heart, and red cells. A high AST is a question, not an answer.
  • Read the two together. The AST/ALT (De Ritis) ratio carries information because the enzymes clear at different speeds; a high ratio (≥2) is classically linked to advanced disease, not merely heavy exposure — but simple folk rules oversimplify it.
  • A single hard or unaccustomed workout can raise AST (and modestly ALT) for up to a week, mimicking liver injury in perfectly healthy people.
  • Timing is part of the result: ask what happened in the 48–72 hours before the draw. For a clean read, skip hard or novel training beforehand.
  • Normal bilirubin, GGT, and ALP alongside raised aminotransferases is a fingerprint that favors a muscle source over liver disease.
  • "In range" reflects a lab's reference population, not your personal optimum — true healthy ceilings are lower than many lab cutoffs.
  • Interpretation is not diagnosis. Persistent, symptomatic, markedly high, or metabolically-flavored patterns warrant medical evaluation.
Looking Ahead

Next, we turn to the kidneys — where creatinine sets up an almost identical trap. Just as AST leaks from muscle and impersonates a liver problem, creatinine is generated by muscle and can make kidney function look worse (or better) than it is depending on how much muscle you carry and how recently you trained. The "read the context" discipline you just practiced twice will pay off a third time, and you will start to feel it becoming automatic.
